intro: A judo jacket, a pair of boxing gloves, a fencing mask, a berimbau, an arnis stick and a mixed martial arts bout sheet can sit on one shelf. Each came from a different place and a different institution. Each has its own founding dates, governing bodies and rule books. This unit asks how to sort and compare them fairly.

First you will sort arts into six working groups: grappling, striking, armed arts made into sport, arts shaped by music and circle, diaspora arts and the modern mix. You will meet the institutions that draw these lines, from the IOC to UNESCO. Then you will compare two arts, judo and taekwondo, by origin, room, nation and code, with capoeira and boxing as a second pair.

By the end, you can explain why a taxonomy is a tool and not a ranking. You can name the laws, federations and dates behind each art. You can also write a comparison that cites its records and marks where legend ends and the documents begin.
bigQuestion: How can we compare martial arts by their rooms, nations and rule books without ranking one above another?

title: Compare Without Ranking

chapters.title: Six Rooms Again
chapters.bigQuestion: How can sorting martial arts into groups help us compare them without claiming one is better?

story.title: Six Objects, One Shelf
story.kicker: A teacher sets six objects on a shelf and asks the class to sort them.
paragraphs: A senior history class in Chicago walks into a room with a long wooden shelf. On it sit six objects. There is a folded judo jacket, a pair of red boxing gloves and a fencing mask with a wire face. There is a berimbau, the one-string musical bow of Afro-Brazilian capoeira. There is a rattan stick from a Filipino arnis club. The last object is a printed bout sheet from a mixed martial arts event.

The teacher hands out index cards. "Sort these into groups," she says. "Then write the rule you used." One group sorts by country: Japan, England, France, Brazil, the Philippines and the United States. Another group sorts by the Olympic Games: the jacket, the gloves and the mask have Olympic events, and the other three do not.

A student named Priya tries a third rule. She sorts by what decides the contest. The jacket goes with grappling. The gloves go with striking. The mask and the stick go with armed arts made into sport. The berimbau does not fit any of those, so she makes a new card for arts shaped by music and a circle.

Then a boy named Mateo asks the question the teacher was waiting for. "Which group is the best one?" The teacher points at the index cards. "Each card answers a different question," she says. "None of them is a ladder." The class looks at the six objects again, now sitting in three different arrangements.
story.think: The class sorted the same six objects three ways. What did each way of sorting show, and what did it hide?

lessons.title: What a Taxonomy Does
lessons.mainIdea: A taxonomy is a system of named groups; it helps us compare things, but every set of groups shows some features and hides others.
reading: In 1735 the Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus published Systema Naturae in Leiden. The book sorted plants and animals into nested groups with names. His system became the model for modern *taxonomy*, the practice of sorting things into named groups by shared features. Scientists still use two-part Latin names that follow his method.

Historians of sport and martial arts sort too. The Olympic Charter sorts the Games into sports, disciplines and events. Wrestling is one sport, for example, and Greco-Roman and freestyle are its two disciplines. Each weight class is a separate event. The groups tell officials who writes which rules and how many medals exist.

Every taxonomy chooses a *criterion*, the single test used to decide where something goes. Sort by country, and capoeira sits with Brazil. Sort by Olympic status, and capoeira sits outside with thousands of other arts. The object is the same; the question changed. Good historians say which criterion they used, so readers can see what the groups show and what they leave out.

words.d: a system for sorting things into named groups by shared features
the single test used to decide which group something belongs in
in the Olympic Charter, a branch of a sport, such as freestyle within wrestling

look.title: One Art, Three Cards
look.text: Card one, sorted by country: capoeira belongs with Brazil. Card two, sorted by Olympic status: capoeira belongs with arts that have no Olympic event. Card three, sorted by music: capoeira belongs with arts where songs and instruments shape the room.
look.prompt: Which card would help a student studying Brazilian law? Which would help a student studying the Olympic program?

check.q: What is a taxonomy?
choices: a system for sorting things into named groups by shared features
a list of champions in order of wins
a rule book for one sport
a ranking of arts from weakest to strongest
check.why: A taxonomy sorts things into named groups by what they share; it is not a ranking.

check.q: Who published Systema Naturae in 1735?
check.why: The Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus published Systema Naturae in 1735.

check.q: In the Olympic Charter's terms, Greco-Roman wrestling is a what?
choices: a discipline of the sport of wrestling
check.why: The Charter sorts wrestling as one sport with two disciplines, Greco-Roman and freestyle.

lessons.title: Groups Are Not a Ladder
lessons.mainIdea: Sorting arts into groups is different from ranking them; the 1993 UFC event was sold as a contest of styles, but a style is a tradition, not a team.
reading: The English word *martial* comes from the Latin martialis, meaning "of Mars," the Roman god of war. Other languages built their own words. Japanese uses budō, often translated "martial way." Chinese uses wushu, written with characters meaning "martial art." Korean musul uses the same two characters. Each word came from its own history, so no single word covers every tradition.

A *ranking* puts things in order from best to worst on one scale. A classification puts things side by side in groups. On November 12, 1993, the first Ultimate Fighting Championship was held at McNichols Sports Arena in Denver, Colorado. Its promoters sold the eight-man tournament as a test of which style was best. Royce Gracie, from a Brazilian family school, won it.

Historians point out that one night in Denver tested eight people under one rule set, not whole traditions. A tradition includes schools, teachers, ranks, rituals and records built over generations. Judo, for example, was founded as an education system in 1882 and became an Olympic sport in 1964. Asking whether judo is "better" than capoeira mixes two different questions about two different institutions.

words.d: having to do with war or fighting; from the Latin for "of Mars"
an order from best to worst on one scale
sorting things side by side into groups without putting them in order

look.title: A Poster and a Record
look.text: A 1993 event poster asks which style is best. A school record book lists a judo school's founding year, its first students, its rank certificates and its teachers for ninety years. Both papers use the word judo.
look.prompt: What kind of question can each paper answer? Why can't the poster answer the record book's question?

check.q: Where does the English word martial come from?
choices: the Latin martialis, meaning of Mars
check.why: Martial comes from the Latin martialis, named for Mars, the Roman god of war.

check.q: How is a ranking different from a classification?
choices: A ranking orders things best to worst; a classification groups them side by side.
A ranking uses groups; a classification uses dates.
A classification always puts the oldest art first.
check.why: A ranking is an order on one scale; a classification sorts into groups without order.

check.q: Where and when was the first Ultimate Fighting Championship held?
check.why: UFC 1 took place at McNichols Sports Arena in Denver on November 12, 1993.

lessons.title: Who Draws the Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Different institutions sort martial arts for different purposes; the IOC sorts for medals, while UNESCO lists arts as living cultural heritage.
reading: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) sorts arts by whether they have an international federation it recognizes. A recognized federation writes the rules and runs world championships. Recognition does not guarantee a place at the Games. Karate, for example, appeared at the Tokyo 2020 Games, held in 2021, and was not on the program for Paris 2024.

UNESCO, the United Nations cultural agency, sorts by a different test. Its *intangible cultural heritage* lists name living practices that communities pass down. Korea's taekkyeon was listed in 2011. The capoeira circle of Brazil was listed in 2014. In 2018 North and South Korea listed ssireum wrestling together, their first joint listing. Pencak silat of Indonesia and silat of Malaysia were both listed in 2019.

The two systems answer different questions. An Olympic listing asks whether an art can be judged the same way in every country. A UNESCO listing asks whether a community keeps a practice alive, with its songs, teachers and gatherings. Taijiquan, listed by UNESCO in 2020, has no Olympic event. That shows no gap in quality; it shows that the two institutions are measuring different things.

words.d: the International Olympic Committee, which runs the Olympic Games and recognizes sport federations
living practices, such as music, crafts or games, that communities pass down; UNESCO keeps lists of them
the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization

look.cite: UNESCO, Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity
look.prompt: Which listing came first? Which was the first joint listing by two countries?

check.q: In what year did UNESCO list the capoeira circle?
check.why: UNESCO inscribed the capoeira circle of Brazil in 2014.

check.q: Which listing was the first joint UNESCO listing by North and South Korea?
check.why: In 2018 the two Koreas listed ssireum wrestling together, their first joint listing.

check.q: What does an IOC-recognized federation do?
choices: It writes the rules and runs world championships for its sport.
It lists living practices as cultural heritage.
It guarantees its sport a place at every Games.
check.why: A recognized federation writes rules and runs championships; recognition does not guarantee a place on the program.

lessons.title: Arts Decided by Holding
lessons.mainIdea: Wrestling, judo and sumo are grappling arts: their contests are decided by gripping and controlling, and each has its own governing body and dates.
reading: Grappling is the name for arts whose contests are decided by gripping and controlling an opponent rather than by hitting. Wrestling is the oldest known example. Scenes of wrestlers appear in Egyptian tomb paintings at Beni Hasan from about 2000 BCE. Wrestling was part of the ancient Olympic Games from 708 BCE, according to Greek records.

At the first modern Olympics in Athens in 1896, Greco-Roman wrestling was on the program. Freestyle wrestling followed at St. Louis in 1904. Their world body was founded in 1912 and took the name *United World Wrestling* in 2014. Judo, founded by Kanō Jigorō in Tokyo in 1882, has its own body, the International Judo Federation (IJF), founded in 1951. Judo first became an Olympic sport at Tokyo in 1964.

Sumo is a grappling art with a very different institution. Professional sumo in Japan is run by the Japan Sumo Association. Its ranking sheet, the banzuke, is published before each tournament. Sumo has no Olympic event. Putting judo and sumo in one group shows what their contests share; it does not make their rooms, rituals or rule books the same.

words.d: arts whose contests are decided by gripping and controlling rather than by hitting
the world governing body for Olympic wrestling, founded in 1912 and renamed in 2014
the ranking sheet of professional sumo, published before each tournament

look.title: Grappling Arts Enter the Modern Olympics
look.unit: year of first Olympic medal event
look.cite: International Olympic Committee, official results database
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first men's judo event and the first women's judo event?

check.q: What makes an art a grappling art?
choices: Its contests are decided by gripping and controlling, not hitting.
It began in the twentieth century.
check.why: Grappling arts are defined by contests decided through gripping and control.

check.q: When did judo first become an Olympic sport?
check.why: Judo debuted at the Tokyo Olympics in 1964; the IJF was founded in 1951.

check.q: Who runs professional sumo in Japan?
check.why: Professional sumo is run by the Japan Sumo Association, which publishes the banzuke.

lessons.title: Arts Decided by Scoring Hits
lessons.mainIdea: Boxing, karate, taekwondo and Muay Thai are striking arts, but each reached the Olympic door at a different time and through a different federation.
reading: Striking is the name for arts whose contests are scored mainly by landing blows. Boxing is the best-documented example in the English-speaking world. The Queensberry Rules of 1867 required gloves and three-minute rounds. Boxing joined the Olympics at St. Louis in 1904. It was left out of the 1912 Stockholm Games because Swedish law banned it at the time.

Taekwondo, shaped in South Korea after 1945 and named in 1955, was a demonstration sport at Seoul in 1988. It became a full medal sport at Sydney in 2000. Its Olympic body, founded in Seoul in 1973, took the name World Taekwondo in 2017. Karate, which grew in Okinawa, reached the Olympics only once, at Tokyo 2020.

Muay Thai is Thailand's national ring sport. Its amateur body, the International Federation of Muaythai Associations (IFMA), won full IOC recognition in 2021. Recognition makes an art eligible to apply for the Games, but Muay Thai has not yet held an Olympic event. Grouping these four as striking arts helps a reader compare them. It does not erase their separate homelands, rule books and federations.

words.d: arts whose contests are scored mainly by landing blows
an organization of national bodies that writes the rules for a sport
a sport shown at an Olympic Games without official medals

look.title: Four Arts, Four Doors
look.text: Boxing: Olympic from 1904, left out in 1912. Taekwondo: demonstration in 1988, medals from 2000. Karate: medals at Tokyo 2020 only. Muay Thai: full IOC recognition in 2021, no Olympic event yet.
look.prompt: All four are striking arts. What does this list show that the word striking alone does not?

check.q: Why was boxing left out of the 1912 Stockholm Olympics?
choices: Swedish law banned boxing at the time.
Boxing had no rule book yet.
The IOC had banned all combat sports.
check.why: Sweden banned boxing then, so it was not held at the 1912 Games.

check.q: When did taekwondo become a full Olympic medal sport?
check.why: Taekwondo was a demonstration sport in 1988 and a medal sport from Sydney 2000.

check.q: What did IFMA receive from the IOC in 2021?
choices: a permanent place at every Games
check.why: IFMA, the amateur Muay Thai body, won full IOC recognition in 2021.

lessons.title: Where the Line Blurs
lessons.mainIdea: Pankration, sambo and sanda mixed holding and hitting long before or outside the modern league, so a two-box chart cannot hold every art.
reading: Some arts never fit one box. Greek records say *pankration* was added to the ancient Olympic Games at Olympia in 648 BCE. Its name means "all strength," and its contests allowed both holding and hitting. Greek vase paintings show pankration bouts watched by judges holding rods. The event ended with the ancient Games themselves in late antiquity.

Sambo was built in the Soviet Union in the 1920s and 1930s from wrestling traditions and judo. Its name is a Russian abbreviation meaning "self-defense without weapons." The Soviet sports committee recognized it as an official sport in 1938. Its world body, the International Sambo Federation (FIAS), received provisional IOC recognition in 2021.

Sanda, also called sanshou, is a Chinese competition code that became standard in the late twentieth century. It allows both kicks and throws inside a raised platform. The International Wushu Federation, founded in 1990, includes sanda in its world championships beside judged forms. A careful chart gives these arts their own row rather than forcing them into grappling or striking.

words.d: an ancient Greek Olympic contest, added in 648 BCE, that allowed holding and hitting
a Soviet sport built in the 1920s and 1930s and recognized officially in 1938
a Chinese competition code, also called sanshou, that allows kicks and throws

look.title: A Row That Won't Fit
look.text: A chart has two columns: grappling and striking. A student tries to add pankration, sambo and sanda. Each one has records showing both holding and hitting in its contests.
look.prompt: Should the student make a third column, or write each art into both columns? Explain your choice.

check.q: When was pankration added to the ancient Olympic Games?
check.why: Greek records date pankration at Olympia to 648 BCE.

check.q: In what year did the Soviet sports committee recognize sambo?
check.why: Sambo was recognized as an official Soviet sport in 1938.

check.q: Which body includes sanda in its world championships?
check.why: The International Wushu Federation, founded in 1990, runs sanda beside judged forms.

lessons.title: Weapons Turned Into Sport
lessons.mainIdea: Fencing, kendo and arnis took old weapon arts and gave them safety equipment, federations and national laws.
reading: Fencing grew from European sword schools and fencing manuals. In the 1800s clubs made it a sport with masks, blunted blades and written rules. Fencing has been held at every modern Olympic Games since Athens in 1896. Its world body, the *FIE* (Fédération Internationale d'Escrime), was founded in Paris in 1913. Women's fencing joined the Olympics at Paris in 1924.

Kendo grew from Japanese sword schools. Practice with bamboo swords and armor spread in the 1700s and 1800s. After 1945 the Allied Occupation restricted martial arts in Japanese schools. The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952. The International Kendo Federation followed in 1970 and held the first World Kendo Championships in Tokyo that year.

Arnis, also called eskrima or kali, is the Filipino art of stick and blade. In December 2009 the Philippines passed Republic Act No. 9850. The law named arnis the national martial art and sport of the Philippines. It also directed schools to include arnis in physical education. An armed art, in this sense, is a history of weapons turned into equipment, rules and school programs.

words.d: the Fédération Internationale d'Escrime, the world fencing body founded in Paris in 1913
the Filipino art of stick and blade, also called eskrima or kali
the 2009 Philippine law naming arnis the national martial art and sport

look.title: A Law Names a National Art
look.text: Arnis is declared the national martial art and sport of the Philippines. The Department of Education is to include it in physical education and sports programs.
look.cite: Republic of the Philippines, Republic Act No. 9850 (Arnis Act of 2009)
look.prompt: What two things does the law do? Which one changes schools?

check.q: Where and when was the FIE founded?
check.why: The world fencing body, the FIE, was founded in Paris in 1913.

check.q: When was the International Kendo Federation founded?
check.why: The International Kendo Federation was founded in 1970; the All Japan Kendo Federation in 1952.

check.q: What did Republic Act No. 9850 do?
choices: It made fencing an Olympic sport.
It named arnis the national martial art and sport of the Philippines.
check.why: The 2009 law made arnis the national martial art and sport and brought it into physical education.

lessons.title: Arts Shaped by Music and Circle
lessons.mainIdea: Capoeira and taijiquan show a group defined less by contest than by the circle, the song, the park and the community that keeps them.
reading: Capoeira grew among enslaved Africans and their descendants in Brazil. Brazil abolished slavery in 1888. Two years later, the Penal Code of 1890 made practicing capoeira in public a crime. In Salvador, Bahia, Manuel dos Reis Machado, called *Mestre* Bimba, opened an academy that won official registration in 1937. Vicente Ferreira Pastinha, Mestre Pastinha, opened a Capoeira Angola center in 1941.

In capoeira the room is the *roda*, a circle of people. The berimbau, a one-string musical bow, leads the songs that open and guide the circle. In 2008 Brazil's national heritage institute, IPHAN, registered capoeira as part of Brazil's cultural heritage. UNESCO listed the capoeira circle in 2014.

Taijiquan is another art often practiced outside any league. Many histories trace it to the Chen family village of Chenjiagou in Henan Province, China. Today millions of people practice it in parks as a health routine. A group for music-and-circle or practice-centered arts lets a reader describe these communities on their own terms, rather than as sports that are missing a scoreboard.

words.d: the circle of people that forms the room in capoeira
Portuguese for master; the title of a senior capoeira teacher
a one-string musical bow that leads the songs in capoeira
Brazil's National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage

look.title: Capoeira in Brazilian Law and Record
rows: Penal Code makes public capoeira a crime

look.prompt: How many years passed between the 1890 ban and the 2008 heritage registration?

check.q: What did Brazil's Penal Code of 1890 do to capoeira?
choices: made practicing it in public a crime
check.why: The 1890 Penal Code made public capoeira a crime, two years after abolition.

check.q: What is the roda in capoeira?
choices: the circle of people that forms the room
check.why: The roda is the circle; the berimbau is the musical bow.

check.q: Where do many histories trace the origin of taijiquan?
choices: the Chen family village of Chenjiagou in Henan
check.why: Many histories trace taijiquan to Chenjiagou, the Chen family village in Henan Province.

lessons.title: Arts That Traveled
lessons.mainIdea: Migration carried arts to new countries, where diaspora communities built new schools that are part of each art's history.
reading: A *diaspora* is a community living far from its homeland that keeps ties to it. In 1908 the ship Kasato Maru brought nearly 800 Japanese immigrants to the port of Santos, Brazil. Japanese judo teachers later traveled and settled in Brazil. The Gracie family's own history says a traveling judo expert, Maeda Mitsuyo, taught Carlos Gracie in Belém. That family account is the root story of Brazilian jiu-jitsu.

Filipino workers began arriving in Hawaii in 1906 to work on sugar plantations. Many later moved to California farm towns such as Stockton, which grew a neighborhood called Little Manila. Arnis teachers in these communities first taught mostly family and friends. In the 1960s, public eskrima schools began to open in California.

After Indonesia won independence from the Netherlands in 1949, many Indo-Dutch families moved to the Netherlands. They brought pencak silat with them, and Dutch silat schools grew from these families. From the 1970s Brazilian capoeira teachers opened schools in the United States and Europe. In each case, the diaspora school is a real branch of the art's history, not a copy of the homeland.

words.d: a community living far from its homeland that keeps ties to it
the ship that brought the first large group of Japanese immigrants to Brazil in 1908
the Filipino neighborhood of Stockton, California

look.prompt: Why might a historian group these three schools together even though they teach different arts?

choices: a community living far from its homeland that keeps ties to it
check.why: A diaspora is a community away from its homeland that keeps ties to it.

check.q: According to the Gracie family's account, who taught Carlos Gracie in Belém?
check.why: The family history names Maeda Mitsuyo, a traveling judo expert, as Carlos Gracie's teacher.

check.q: Who brought pencak silat to the Netherlands?
choices: Japanese immigrants on the Kasato Maru

check.why: After 1949, Indo-Dutch families carried pencak silat to the Netherlands.

sections.title: Mixed Rooms and the Limits of a Chart

lessons.title: The Modern Mix
lessons.mainIdea: Mixed martial arts became a regulated league when state commissions adopted the Unified Rules in 2001 and 2009.
reading: Before the UFC, Brazil had vale tudo, Portuguese for "anything goes." These twentieth-century events let athletes from different arts meet under few rules. The first UFC in Denver in 1993 drew on that model. Early events had no weight classes and very few rules, and several U.S. states refused to allow them.

In 2000 the New Jersey State Athletic Control Board drafted rules for mixed martial arts, and it adopted them in 2001. They set weight classes, rounds, gloves and a list of fouls. In 2009 the Association of Boxing Commissions adopted these *Unified Rules* for its member commissions across the country. A *commission* is a government board that licenses athletes and approves events.

Mixed martial arts, or MMA, belongs in its own group. It is a modern league that borrows athletes from wrestling, boxing, judo, Brazilian jiu-jitsu and Muay Thai. Its authority comes from state commissions and private promoters, not from a founder's lineage or a national ministry. Placing MMA in a "modern mix" group shows how its institution differs from the older rooms it draws on.

words.d: Portuguese for "anything goes"; Brazilian events that matched athletes from different arts
the rules for mixed martial arts drafted in New Jersey and adopted nationally in 2009
a government board that licenses athletes and approves events

look.title: A Stamp on a Bout Sheet
look.text: A bout sheet from 1993 lists eight names and no weight classes. A bout sheet from 2010 lists weight classes, round lengths, a referee's license number and a state commission stamp.
look.prompt: What changed between the two sheets, and which institution made the change?

check.q: What does vale tudo mean?
check.why: Vale tudo is Portuguese for anything goes.

check.q: Which body adopted the Unified Rules for its member commissions in 2009?
check.why: The Association of Boxing Commissions adopted the Unified Rules in 2009.

check.q: Where does MMA's authority mainly come from?
check.why: MMA is governed by state commissions and run by private promoters.

lessons.title: Federations by Founding Date
lessons.mainIdea: The world bodies that govern martial sports were founded across most of the twentieth century, so the modern map took shape step by step.
reading: A useful criterion for sorting is the year each world body was founded. Wrestling's world body dates to 1912 and fencing's FIE to 1913. The International Amateur Boxing Association, AIBA, was founded in 1946. It renamed itself the International Boxing Association, IBA, in 2021.

The IJF followed in 1951. The World Union of Karate-do Organizations was founded in 1970 and later became the World Karate Federation. The World Taekwondo Federation was founded in 1973. Each founding set up a rule book that national bodies agreed to follow, which is why a judo or fencing contest looks the same in Chicago and in Tokyo.

Founding dates can also end. In 2023 the IOC withdrew its recognition of the IBA after years of disputes over governance and judging. A new body, World Boxing, was formed the same year. A chart of founding years helps a reader see that *governance*, the way an organization is run, is itself part of each art's history.

words.d: the way an organization is run and makes its decisions
the International Amateur Boxing Association, founded in 1946 and renamed IBA in 2021
a boxing federation formed in 2023

lessons.title: What Every Chart Hides
lessons.mainIdea: One art can sit in several groups at once and can change groups over time, so a taxonomy is a tool for questions, not a final answer.
reading: Judo shows how an art can change groups. Kanō Jigorō founded it in 1882 as a system of physical and moral education. In 1911 Japan's Ministry of Education allowed judo in middle schools. In 1964 it became an Olympic sport. The same art sat in the education group, then the school group, then the Olympic group, as its institutions changed.

Other arts sit in two groups at once. Capoeira belongs with music-and-circle arts and also with diaspora arts, since schools now operate on several continents. Arnis is an armed art and also a national school subject under a 2009 law. Muay Thai is a striking sport and also a national symbol in Thailand. The wai khru ram muay, a ceremony of respect to teachers performed before bouts, belongs to its history.

Historians call a system that admits these overlaps a *heuristic*: a tool that helps you ask better questions. A six-group chart of grappling, striking, armed, music-and-circle, diaspora and modern mix is a heuristic. It lets a student line up two arts side by side and compare rooms, codes and dates. It never tells the student which art is worth more.

words.d: a tool or rule of thumb that helps you ask better questions or find answers
a ceremony of respect to teachers performed before Muay Thai bouts
when one thing belongs to two or more groups at the same time

chapters.title: Capstone Compare
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a historian compare two martial arts fairly, using origins, rooms, nations and rule books with dates?

story.title: Two Rule Books, One Page Each
story.kicker: Two students open two rule books to the page that says who may compete.
paragraphs: Two seniors sit at a library table in Illinois with a stack of printouts. Jasmine has the International Judo Federation's rules for competition. Andre has World Taekwondo's competition rules. Their assignment is to compare the two arts without saying which one is better.

Jasmine finds the page on weight categories. It lists seven categories for men and seven for women at the Olympic Games. It also names the rules on judogi, the judo uniform, and on which athlete wears blue. Andre finds the matching page in his book. At the Olympics, taekwondo uses four weight categories for each sex, and athletes wear electronic trunk protectors.

They look at the covers. The judo rule book comes from a body founded in 1951, which carries an art founded in Tokyo in 1882. The taekwondo rule book comes from a body founded in Seoul in 1973, carrying an art named in 1955. Jasmine writes the four dates in a column. Andre adds the Olympic years beside them: 1964 for judo and 2000 for taekwondo.

"So the two pages look alike," Andre says, "but the histories behind them do not." Jasmine nods and draws a line down the middle of a clean sheet. At the top of one side she writes Origin. Below it she writes Room, then Nation, then Code. Andre starts filling in his side.
story.think: Why might two rule books that look alike still come from very different histories?

lessons.title: Two Founding Dates
lessons.mainIdea: Judo has a single founder and a founding year, 1882; taekwondo took its name in 1955 from a group of Korean schools, so the two origins have different shapes.
reading: Kanō Jigorō was born in 1860 in Mikage, near Kobe. As a university student in Tokyo he trained in two jujutsu schools, Tenjin Shin'yō-ryū and Kitō-ryū. In 1882 he opened the *Kodokan* in a small room at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. He called his system judo, "the gentle way." Judo therefore has one founder, one place and one year.

Taekwondo's origin has a different shape. Korea was under Japanese colonial rule from 1910 to 1945. In the 1940s several *kwan*, or schools, opened in Seoul, and many of their founders had trained in karate in Japan. In 1955 a committee of teachers and military officers chose the name taekwondo, meaning roughly "the way of the foot and the fist."

Comparing the two origins does not mean judging them. Judo began as one man's education system. Taekwondo began as a union of several schools that later agreed on a national name and standard. A historian writes both shapes down with their dates, then asks what each shape meant for later arguments about who owns the art.

words.d: the judo school Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882; still judo's headquarters
Korean for school or hall; the early schools that joined to form taekwondo
control of one country by another; Japan ruled Korea from 1910 to 1945

lessons.title: Older Roots Named Carefully
lessons.mainIdea: Both arts had older arts behind them, and a fair comparison names those roots with dates instead of treating either art as appearing from nothing.
reading: Jujutsu was a family of Japanese schools, called *koryū*, or old-style schools. Many took shape during the Edo period, from 1603 to 1868. Each koryū passed down its teaching through a line of headmasters and written scrolls. When samurai lost their status in the Meiji era, many jujutsu schools lost students. Kanō gathered material from two of them and built judo as a modern school subject.

Korea also had older practices. Taekkyeon was a Korean folk game recorded in the late Joseon period, the dynasty that ruled until 1897. A few teachers kept it alive through colonial rule, and South Korea named it an Important Intangible Cultural Property in 1983. UNESCO listed taekkyeon in 2011. Taekwondo and taekkyeon share a country and a syllable, but they have separate institutions.

Naming roots carefully means naming their limits too. Kanō's judo borrowed from jujutsu but changed its purpose and its ranks. Historians still debate how much taekwondo drew on taekkyeon versus on karate. A good comparison states what the record shows and marks where scholars disagree.

words.d: Japanese for old-style schools; martial schools founded before the Meiji era
a Korean folk game recorded in the Joseon period and listed by UNESCO in 2011
the era of Japanese history from 1603 to 1868

look.text: Tree one: two Edo-period jujutsu schools, then Kanō's Kodokan in 1882. Tree two: Korean taekkyeon, karate learned in Japan during colonial rule, the kwan of the 1940s, then the name taekwondo in 1955. A dotted line marks each branch that historians still debate.
look.prompt: Which branches in each tree have strong records? Which get a dotted line, and why?

check.why: Scholars debate the balance of taekkyeon and karate in taekwondo's formation.

lessons.title: Legend Beside Record
lessons.mainIdea: Origin stories and documents answer different questions, so a careful comparison labels legends as legends and sets them beside dated records.
reading: Many taekwondo histories point to murals in Goguryeo tombs near Ji'an, in today's northeast China. The murals date from about the fifth century and show figures in paired poses. Some writers present them as early taekwondo. Historians say the murals show that Koreans of that era practiced combat arts. They cannot show a direct line to a sport named in 1955.

Capoeira has well-known origin stories too. One popular story says enslaved Africans disguised fighting as dance to hide it from enslavers. Scholars treat this as a *legend*: an old story that people tell, not a documented event. What the record shows is different. Police records from nineteenth-century Rio de Janeiro list arrests for capoeira, and the 1890 Penal Code banned it in public.

Judo's record is unusually full because Kanō wrote about his own work. The Kodokan kept records of students and ranks from its first years. Even so, stories grew around its early matches. A fair comparison puts each art's legends and records in two columns, with a *primary source* such as a law, a police record or a founder's writing named for every dated claim.

words.d: an old story that people tell, which may not be a documented event
a record made at the time, such as a law, a police record or a founder's own writing
an ancient Korean kingdom whose tombs near Ji'an contain painted murals

look.title: Two Columns

look.prompt: What can Column B prove that Column A cannot? What might Column A still tell a historian about memory?

check.q: What can the Goguryeo tomb murals show, according to historians?
choices: that taekwondo was named in the fifth century
that Koreans of that era practiced combat arts
check.why: The murals show combat arts in that era but not a direct line to modern taekwondo.

check.q: Why do scholars call the story of capoeira hidden in dance a legend?
choices: It is a told story, not a documented event.

check.why: A legend is a story people tell; the documents show arrests and a ban instead.

check.q: Which is a primary source for capoeira's history?
choices: a nineteenth-century Rio de Janeiro police record
check.why: A police record made at the time is a primary source.

lessons.title: Comparing the Rooms
lessons.mainIdea: The room is a rule you can see: the dojo and its mats, the dojang, the boxing ring and the capoeira circle each came from a named history.
reading: The *dojo* is the Japanese word for a practice hall; it originally meant a place for Buddhist practice. Kanō's first Kodokan room held twelve tatami mats. Tatami are woven straw mats used as flooring in Japanese homes. Judo rooms kept the tatami, and today competition mats are made of foam built to the same idea.

Taekwondo schools use the Korean word *dojang*, written with the same characters as dojo. Many Korean dojang display the South Korean flag beside the school's certificates. At the Olympics, taekwondo moved from a square competition area to an octagon in the 2010s. Each change was written into World Taekwondo's competition rules.

Boxing and capoeira show other rooms. The Queensberry Rules of 1867 began by describing a 24-foot ring. Capoeira needs no built room at all; its circle is made of people, songs and a berimbau, and it can form in a street or a hall. Comparing rooms tells a historian who paid for the space, who could enter and which rule book governed it.

words.d: Japanese for practice hall; originally a place for Buddhist practice
Korean for practice hall, used by taekwondo schools
woven straw mats used as flooring in Japan and in early judo rooms

check.why: Dojo first meant a place for Buddhist practice, then a practice hall.

check.why: Rule 1 of the Queensberry Rules calls for a 24-foot ring, or as near as practicable.

choices: a circle of people, songs and a berimbau

check.why: Capoeira's roda is formed by people and music, not a built space.

lessons.title: The Nation and the Name
lessons.mainIdea: Japan and South Korea both tied their arts to the nation, but at different times and through different laws and institutions.
reading: Judo grew alongside the Meiji state's push to build modern schools. The Dai Nippon Butokukai, a national martial arts body, was founded in Kyoto in 1895. In 1911 judo entered middle school programs as an allowed subject, and in 1931 judo or kendo became required for boys. After 1945 the Allied Occupation stopped budo in Japanese schools. Judo returned to schools as a sport in 1950.

Taekwondo became a symbol of South Korea after the Korean War. The Kukkiwon, called the World Taekwondo Headquarters, opened in Seoul in 1972. It issues dan certificates, the black-belt ranks, to students around the world. In 2018 South Korea passed a law naming taekwondo its national sport.

Choi Hong-hi, the army general credited with proposing the name in 1955, founded the International Taekwon-Do Federation (ITF) in 1966. He moved to Canada in 1972 after conflict with South Korea's government. The ITF later built ties with North Korea. So taekwondo has two major federations, each with its own rules, while judo has one world federation. The *nation* shaped both arts, but in different ways.

words.d: a people with a shared government and identity; a state
a national Japanese martial arts body founded in Kyoto in 1895
the International Taekwon-Do Federation, founded by Choi Hong-hi in 1966
the World Taekwondo Headquarters in Seoul, opened in 1972; it issues dan certificates

look.text: Japan: a national martial arts body in 1895, school judo in 1911, required budo for boys in 1931, a ban after 1945, a return as sport in 1950. South Korea: a name in 1955, a split in 1966, a national headquarters in 1972, a national sport law in 2018.

check.why: After budo was stopped in 1945, judo returned to schools as a sport in 1950.

check.why: General Choi Hong-hi founded the ITF in 1966.

check.why: The Kukkiwon issues dan certificates to taekwondo students worldwide.

lessons.title: Arts the State Pushed Away
lessons.mainIdea: Not every art was built by a nation; capoeira and English prizefighting were first pushed out by law before new institutions took them in.
reading: Capoeira's relationship with the state began with punishment. The 1890 Penal Code banned it in public. In the 1930s, under President Getúlio Vargas, the government began to promote Brazilian national culture. Mestre Bimba's academy won official registration in 1937, and capoeira moved into registered schools. By 2008 the state had registered it as national heritage.

English prizefighting followed a similar path from outlaw to rule book. Bare-knuckle prize fights were illegal in Britain for much of the 1800s, and crowds gathered in secret. The Queensberry Rules of 1867 added gloves and timed rounds. In 1880 the Amateur Boxing Association was founded in England to run amateur boxing under written rules.

These cases change a comparison. Judo and taekwondo were built partly with state support. Capoeira and boxing were first treated as problems, and their institutions grew as a response to *prohibition*, a legal ban. A fair comparison asks the same question of every art: what did the law do to this room, and when?

words.d: a legal ban on an activity
boxing for money, often illegal in Britain in the 1800s
the body founded in England in 1880 to run amateur boxing

choices: a legal ban on an activity
check.why: Prohibition means a legal ban.

check.why: The Amateur Boxing Association was founded in 1880.

check.why: Under Getúlio Vargas, the government promoted national culture, and Bimba's academy was registered in 1937.

lessons.title: Who May Start
lessons.mainIdea: A rule book decides who may compete by weight, sex and age; women entered each Olympic martial sport in a different year.
reading: A *weight category* is a class that groups athletes by body weight so that similar sizes compete. At the Paris 2024 Olympics, judo held seven categories for each sex. Taekwondo held four for each sex. Freestyle wrestling held six for each sex. Boxing held seven for men and six for women. Each number comes from a deal between a federation and the IOC about how many athletes the Games can hold.

The same pages record when women could start. Women's fencing joined the Olympics in 1924. Women's judo became a medal event in 1992, after a demonstration in 1988. Taekwondo included women from its first medal Games in 2000. Women's wrestling followed in 2004 and women's boxing in 2012.

In the United States, *Title IX* of the Education Amendments of 1972 banned sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money. School and college programs opened slowly after it. In Illinois, the IHSA held its first boys wrestling state finals in 1937 and its first girls wrestling state finals in 2022. Every "who may start" page has a date behind it.

words.d: a class that groups athletes by body weight so similar sizes compete
part of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bans sex discrimination in federally funded education programs
the Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900, which runs high school sports in Illinois

check.why: Olympic taekwondo uses four weight categories for each sex.

check.why: Women's judo was a demonstration in 1988 and a medal event from 1992.

check.q: When did the IHSA hold its first girls wrestling state finals?
check.why: The IHSA's first girls wrestling state finals came in 2022; boys began in 1937.

lessons.title: Who Writes the Rules and Ranks
lessons.mainIdea: Judo and taekwondo split authority between a headquarters that grants ranks and a federation that runs competition.
reading: Kanō Jigorō created the *dan* ranking system for judo. In 1883 he awarded the first shodan, or first-degree rank, to two students, Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō. The black belt later became the visible sign of dan rank. The Kodokan still grants dan ranks, and many national judo bodies grant them too.

Competition rules are a separate job. The IJF writes judo's contest rules and runs the World Championships and Olympic events. In taekwondo, the Kukkiwon grants dan certificates, while World Taekwondo writes the competition rules. The ITF keeps its own rules and ranks. A student can therefore hold a rank from one body and compete under another body's rules.

Kanō also served the Olympic movement. In 1909 he became the first IOC member from Asia. He died in 1938, decades before judo entered the Games in 1964. Comparing *authority* means asking which body has the power to decide each question: rank, rules, uniform or who may enter.

words.d: a numbered rank for advanced students; first dan is shodan
first-degree dan rank; first awarded in judo in 1883
the recognized power to make decisions and rules

look.text: A taekwondo athlete holds a dan certificate from the Kukkiwon in Seoul. She enters an Olympic qualifier run under World Taekwondo's competition rules. A judo athlete holds a Kodokan dan certificate and enters an IJF World Championship.
look.prompt: For each athlete, which body decided the rank and which body decided the rules of the contest?

check.why: Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō received the first shodan in 1883.

check.q: In taekwondo, which body writes the Olympic competition rules?
check.why: World Taekwondo writes the competition rules; the Kukkiwon grants dan certificates.

check.q: When did Kanō Jigorō become the first IOC member from Asia?
check.why: Kanō joined the IOC in 1909 as its first member from Asia.

lessons.title: Rule Books That Changed
lessons.mainIdea: Rule books are revised over time, so a comparison must say which edition and which year it describes.
reading: Rule books are revised in numbered or dated editions. In judo, the IJF approved a blue *judogi*, the judo uniform, in the late 1990s so that judges and audiences could tell the two athletes apart. Before that, both athletes wore white and were marked by colored belts. Dutch champion Anton Geesink, who won the open-weight gold at Tokyo in 1964, was among its best-known supporters.

Taekwondo changed its scoring technology. After arguments over judging, World Taekwondo introduced electronic trunk protectors that register scoring contact. The London 2012 Olympics used this protector and scoring system, together with instant video replay. The change was written into the federation's competition rules.

Because rules change, a historian always names the *edition*, meaning the version and year of a rule book. A claim like "judo athletes wear white" was true in 1964 and not true at every event after the 1990s. Citing the year keeps a comparison accurate.

words.d: the jacket and trousers worn in judo
one version of a rule book, marked by a number or a year
a recorded view that officials can review before a decision

look.title: Same Art, Two Years
look.text: A 1964 photo shows two judo athletes in white at the Tokyo Olympics. A photo from a recent Olympics shows one athlete in white and one in blue. A 2008 taekwondo scoresheet was filled in by judges; a 2012 scoresheet was printed from electronic protectors.
look.prompt: What would a student get wrong by describing either art from only one of these photos or sheets?

choices: so judges and audiences could tell the two athletes apart
check.why: The blue judogi made it easier to tell the two athletes apart.

check.q: Which Olympics used taekwondo's electronic protector and scoring system with instant replay?
check.why: London 2012 used electronic trunk protectors and instant video replay.

check.q: What is an edition of a rule book?
choices: a summary written by a fan
one version of the rule book, marked by a number or year
check.why: An edition is a dated or numbered version of a rule book.

lessons.title: A Frame From Ritual to Record
lessons.mainIdea: Allen Guttmann's 1978 book From Ritual to Record gives historians named features for comparing sports without ranking them.
reading: In 1978 the historian Allen Guttmann published From Ritual to Record: The Nature of Modern Sports. He listed seven features that mark modern sport. They are secularism, equality, specialization, rationalization, bureaucracy, quantification and the quest for records. Bureaucracy means running an activity through offices and officials with written rules.

Guttmann's list works as a comparison frame. Judo after 1951 shows strong bureaucracy: an international federation, written rules and world championships. Capoeira in a roda shows weaker bureaucracy but strong ties to music and community. Quantification, turning performance into numbers, is high in taekwondo's electronic scoring and low in a capoeira circle, which has no scoreboard.

Guttmann described these features; he did not claim modern sport was better than older practice. Other historians have criticized his list for fitting European sport better than other traditions. That debate is useful. A student can use the frame to line up two arts and then say where the frame fits and where it does not.

words.d: running an activity through offices and officials with written rules
turning performance into numbers, such as points or times
separation from religious ritual or purpose

look.title: Seven Features of Modern Sport
look.text: Modern sports are marked by secularism, equality of opportunity, specialization of roles, rationalization, bureaucratic organization, quantification and the quest for records.
look.cite: Allen Guttmann, From Ritual to Record: The Nature of Modern Sports (Columbia University Press, 1978)
look.prompt: Pick two arts from this unit. Which of the seven features fits each one strongly, and which weakly?

check.q: Who wrote From Ritual to Record in 1978?
check.why: The historian Allen Guttmann published From Ritual to Record in 1978.

check.q: What does quantification mean?
check.why: Quantification turns performance into numbers, such as points.

check.q: What criticism have other historians made of Guttmann's list?
choices: It fits European sport better than other traditions.
It was written before the modern Olympics.
check.why: Critics say the list fits European sport better than other traditions.

lessons.title: Citing the Record
lessons.mainIdea: A strong comparison cites named records for every date: founding documents, rule book editions, laws and official results.
reading: Each institution in this unit keeps records a historian can cite. The Kodokan in Bunkyō, Tokyo, keeps a library and a museum of judo history. The IJF publishes its Sports and Organisation Rules. World Taekwondo publishes its Competition Rules and Interpretation. The IOC keeps official results for every Games, and its Olympic Studies Centre in Lausanne, Switzerland, holds archives.

Laws are records too. Republic Act No. 9850 of 2009 can be cited for arnis. The 1890 Brazilian Penal Code can be cited for capoeira's ban. Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 can be cited for school programs in the United States. A *citation* names who made the record, what it is and when it was made.

A *secondary source* is a later work that studies primary sources, such as Guttmann's book. Strong comparisons use both kinds and say which is which. Kanō's own writings, gathered in English as Kodokan Judo in 1986, are a primary source for his aims. A historian's study of the Kodokan is a secondary source. Naming both lets a reader check every claim.

words.d: a note naming who made a record, what it is and when
a later work that studies primary sources
a place that keeps original records for research

look.title: Match the Claim to the Record
look.text: Claim 1: arnis is the national martial art of the Philippines. Claim 2: women's judo became an Olympic medal event in 1992. Claim 3: capoeira was banned in public in 1890. Records: IOC official results; Republic Act No. 9850; Brazil's Código Penal of 1890.
look.prompt: Match each claim to the record you would cite. Which records are laws?

check.q: What is a secondary source?
choices: a law passed by a government
a police record from the time
a later work that studies primary sources
check.why: A secondary source studies primary sources after the fact.

check.q: Where is the IOC's Olympic Studies Centre?
check.why: The Olympic Studies Centre is in Lausanne, where the IOC is based.

check.q: Which record would you cite for capoeira's 1890 ban?
check.why: The Brazilian Penal Code of 1890 made public capoeira a crime.

review.q: Which statement compares the origins of judo and taekwondo accurately?
choices: Judo had one founder in 1882; taekwondo took its name in 1955 from a union of several schools.
Both were founded by Kanō Jigorō.
Taekwondo is older than judo by a century.
Both were founded at the Kukkiwon.
review.why: Kanō founded judo in 1882; the kwan agreed on the name taekwondo in 1955.

review.q: What is the difference between a legend and a primary source?
choices: A legend is a law; a primary source is a story.
A legend is a told story; a primary source is a record made at the time.
A primary source is always a movie.
review.why: Legends are stories people tell; primary sources are records made at the time.

review.q: Which pair of arts in this chapter was first pushed away by law?
review.why: Capoeira was banned in 1890, and bare-knuckle prizefighting was illegal in Britain for much of the 1800s.

review.q: Which body grants taekwondo dan certificates?
review.why: The Kukkiwon in Seoul issues dan certificates; World Taekwondo writes competition rules.

review.q: Why does taekwondo have two major federations?
choices: Choi Hong-hi founded the ITF in 1966, separate from the body later called World Taekwondo.
The IOC created two versions in 2000.
review.why: The ITF, founded in 1966, and World Taekwondo, founded in 1973, keep separate rules.

review.q: When did women's boxing join the Olympic Games?
review.why: Women's boxing joined the Olympics in 2012.

review.q: Why should a comparison name a rule book's edition?
choices: Rules change over time, such as the blue judogi and electronic scoring.
review.why: Rules are revised, so a claim is true only for a given edition and year.

review.q: Which feature from Guttmann's list is high in taekwondo's electronic scoring and low in a capoeira circle?
review.why: Electronic scoring turns performance into numbers; a roda has no scoreboard.
